newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Diversity, returns make funds big hitters in softs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Diversity, returns make funds big hitters in softs.

text.p: Funds looking to hold diversified portfolios have in the past few years found a new home for their money -- soft commodities.
"It's a diversification tactic," said a trader here with a U.S. firm.

"The added attraction is that the activity in commodities can produce substantial moves. Prices could double in a few months," he said, noting that it is harder to get that type of movement in financial markets. "How often do you see bond prices double in a few months?"

Funds have grown so much over the past few years that they are collectively powerful enough to swing commodity prices sharply, especially for the "soft" or tropical commodities led by coffee, cocoa and sugar.

Last month, coffee futures tumbled sharply on what traders said was fund selling. The following week, massive fund liquidation in cocoa was said to have forced prices down more than five percent in one afternoon.
Softs turnover has steadily risen at the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE).
In 1996, LIFFE cocoa, dollar-denominated robusta coffee and white sugar traded about 3.5 million futures, up from about 3.2 million in 1993 and 2.0 million in 1991.
In the first quarter, LIFFE soft commodities traded 1.1 million futures, outpacing 1996's first-quarter 941,957 total.

Though some of the volume increase is attributed to more origin hedging and industry and trade buying, the higher turnover reflects an overall trend in softs that includes funds, said Philip O'Neill, associate director at Union Cal.
VOLATILITY SPURS TURNOVER
Fund managers said more fund money has flowed into soft commodities for various reasons, including the jump in volatility and speculative opportunities in the past few years.
O'Neill said higher volatility spurs institutions to use the markets to hedge, which in turn, helps attract locals and funds.

In 1994, frost damaged the Brazilian coffee crop, sending world prices soaring and volatility to about 83 percent near the third week of August 1994 on weekly charts. That compares with a low of about 12.5 percent hit at the end of February 1994.

Last year in cocoa, good weather pushed the Ivory Coast's production to a record 1.2 million tonnes to flood the market with excess supply. That helped boost volatilities to about 20.0 percent in September and October on monthly charts from a low of about 16 percent in May 1993.
Nevertheless, analysts continue to forecast cocoa deficits in coming years because of expected increases in consumption in Eastern Europe and other developing countries as their economies get richer.
A large trading house is also believed to have accumulated about a third of the world's cocoa last summer. The squeeze lifted volatilities to about 21 percent in August and September.

This year, speculation over the Ivorian crop size and fears that the trading house could influence prices by releasing its cocoa at any time continue to keep volatilities buoyed. In April, nearby volatilities lingered near 30 percent.
FUNDS TRADE ON TRENDS
Fund managers estimate more than 90 percent of funds are mechanical and systems-based, following technicals and trends.

"The vast majority are technical traders," said a trader here with a Dutch bank. Commodity trading advisors (CTAs) "like to say they look at fundamentals but really, they look at so many commodities that they have to be mostly technical traders."
As long as the market has a trend, funds will trade it.
"Coffee, bunds, sugar, Nikkei -- the risk is the same, the name is different," a U.S. trader said. "If volume is there, it is tradeable. It doesn't matter what it is."
But "you have to be slightly more careful (in softs) because the liquidity is smaller," said the Dutch bank trader.
Lower liquidity does not deter large, private wealth funds from trading softs for short-, medium- or long-term gains.

Because softs markets are not as deep as financial markets or even other commodity markets, traders said funds placing large-sized orders will simply execute them in chunks over time, careful to avoid slippage, or pushing prices against themselves.
Funds can also manage a billion dollars and trade softs because "the amounts invested in softs varies," O'Neill said. "It's probably only part of the overall portfolio."
FORECASTS FOR FURTHER GROWTH
Though most growth has concentrated in the U.S., fund managers see it spreading as other markets expand and other exchanges, like LIFFE, grab more business for themselves.
Traders also expect the overall amount of money funneled into softs to rise as money under management grows in general.

"There's huge potential in this market," O'Neill said. "Look at the emerging markets of Latin America, China and the Far East. As those markets develop, there will be more money coming into the market."
Once futures see more liquidity flowing in, fund managers expect options to follow and become a more common hedging and speculative tool to protect portfolios or enhance gains.
LIFFE softs options tallied 58,710 in the first quarter, up from 52,061 a year ago.
